subject: physics
title: Resistance and I-V characteristics
key_idea: Resistance is potential difference divided by current, R = V / I. Ohm's law says the current in a metal at constant temperature is directly proportional to the p.d. An I-V graph shows how a component behaves, and only a straight line through the origin means a constant resistance.

blocks.text: Resistance measures how hard it is to push current through a component. It is defined for every component, whether or not it obeys Ohm's law.

items.meaning: The potential difference across a component divided by the current in it.
The unit of resistance. One ohm is one volt per ampere.
For a metallic conductor at constant temperature, the current is directly proportional to the potential difference across it.
A conductor that obeys Ohm's law, so its resistance is constant.

items: Ohm's law is a special case: I ∝ V only while the temperature and other physical conditions stay constant.
R = V / I is a definition. It does not mean that V and I are proportional.
Unless a question says otherwise, treat an ammeter as ideal (zero resistance) and a voltmeter as ideal (infinite resistance).
R = V / I always defines resistance.
Ohm's law holds only at constant temperature, and only for ohmic conductors.
Ideal ammeter: zero resistance. Ideal voltmeter: infinite resistance.

blocks.text: An I-V characteristic plots current against p.d. for a component. Its shape shows how the resistance changes.

rows: Resistor or metal wire at constant temperature
Curve that flattens as p.d. rises, symmetric about the origin
Almost zero current in reverse and below about 0.6 V forward, then a steep rise
Very high in reverse, falls sharply once conducting
Like a diode but with a higher forward threshold; it emits light when it conducts
Very high in reverse, falls sharply once conducting
Curve that steepens as current heats it

diagram.alt: Pick a component to see what its I-V graph looks like and how its resistance changes.

options.label: Filament lamp
results: Increases, because the filament gets hotter

options.label: Semiconductor diode
results: Flat, then a steep rise in the forward direction only
Very high until the threshold, then it falls

options.label: NTC thermistor
results: Decreases, because more carriers are released as it warms

items: Only a straight line through the origin shows constant resistance.
A diode conducts in one direction only, above a threshold p.d.
A filament lamp's resistance increases and a thermistor's decreases as current rises.

blocks.text: The resistance of a filament lamp increases as the current increases, because its temperature increases.

items.text: A larger current transfers more energy to the filament each second, so its temperature rises.
The metal ions vibrate with larger amplitude.
The conduction electrons collide with the ions more often.
The current rises less than in proportion to the p.d., so R = V / I increases.

items: Read resistance at a point from the values of V and I there: R = V / I.
Do not use the gradient of a curve. With I on the y-axis, the gradient of a straight line through the origin is 1 ÷ R.
If V is on the y-axis, the gradient of a straight line through the origin is R itself.
Higher temperature means more frequent electron-ion collisions and a larger resistance.
For a curve, find R at a point as V divided by I, not from the slope.

checks.a: The current in a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the temperature stays constant.

checks.q: Explain why the I-V graph of a filament lamp is a curve that flattens at high p.d.
checks.a: A larger current makes the filament hotter. The ions vibrate more and collide with the electrons more often, so the resistance increases. Current then rises less than in proportion to p.d.

checks.q: At 4.0 V a lamp carries 0.50 A, and at 8.0 V it carries 0.70 A. Calculate its resistance at each p.d. and say whether it is ohmic.
checks.a: At 4.0 V: R = 4.0 ÷ 0.50 = 8.0 Ω. At 8.0 V: R = 8.0 ÷ 0.70 = 11 Ω. The resistance changes, so it is not ohmic.

items: Questions can put either I or V on the horizontal axis. Work out which axis is which before reading a gradient.
Treat meters as ideal unless the question says otherwise.
Ohm's law is a special case of I ∝ V under constant physical conditions, not a definition of resistance.

blocks.text: You must know how to investigate the characteristics of ohmic and non-ohmic components.

items.text: Put the component in series with an ammeter and connect a voltmeter across it only.
Use a variable resistor as a potential divider, or a variable supply, to change the p.d. from zero in small steps.
Read V and I at each step. Reverse the connections to cover negative values.
Keep the current low enough that the component does not overheat or burn out. Put a protective resistor in series with a diode or LED.
Enter the results in a spreadsheet, plot I against V, and calculate V / I for each row to see how R changes.
